# Cross-Account Permissions: Delegating Access to a User in Another Account

An AWS account can grant another AWS account permission to access its resources, such as buckets and objects. Account B can then delegate the permissions it received from Account A to users in its own account. Alternatively, Account A can directly grant a user in Account B permissions using a bucket policy. Granting permissions to IAM roles is a better practice than granting them to individual users.

For a user in Account B to access a resource owned by Account A, the user needs permission from two sources. The user needs permission from the resource owner (Account A), and also from the parent account (Account B). Only when the user has permission from the resource owner and permission from the parent account can the user access the resource. Permissions can be granted by an ACL, a bucket policy, or a user policy.

## Walkthrough overview

The Account A administrator attaches a bucket policy granting cross-account permissions to Account B. The bucket policy grants s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket permissions to Account B. The administrator user in Account B automatically inherits the permissions granted to Account B. The Account B administrator then attaches a user policy to the user, delegating the permissions received from Account A.

The walkthrough does not use root user credentials. Instead, it uses an administrator user in each account to create resources and grant permissions. The tasks of creating users and granting permissions are done in the AWS Management Console. The walkthrough uses the AWS CLI and AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell to verify permissions.

## Verifying delegated permissions

The Account B administrator creates user Dave in Account B. Dave has an inline policy allowing only s3:ListBucket on the bucket. Because Account A's bucket policy allows Account B s3:ListBucket access, and Account B delegates that permission to Dave, Dave can list the contents of the bucket owned by Account A. Dave does not have any permissions other than s3:ListBucket. So when Dave runs get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, Amazon S3 returns permission denied.

## Optional test: explicit deny

An explicit deny in a bucket policy or user policy takes precedence over any other permissions. In the optional test, the bucket policy explicitly denies Account B the s3:ListBucket permission, even though the bucket policy otherwise grants Account B that permission. As a result, Account B and its users cannot list objects in the bucket. Access is denied for AccountBadmin listing the bucket in the explicit deny test.

# Granting cross-account bucket permissions to a user in another account

## Before you begin

You need the following in place before starting the walkthrough:

- Two AWS accounts, referred to here as Account A and Account B (steps at the linked page).
- An administrator IAM user named AccountAadmin in Account A, with a full-access policy. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_users_create.html
- An administrator IAM user named AccountBadmin in Account B, with a full-access policy. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_users_create.html
- The AWS CLI or AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell installed, with the profiles AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin configured. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/policy-eval-walkthrough-download-awscli.html

## Concepts

An AWS account can grant another AWS account permission to access its resources, such as buckets and objects. Only after that grant has happened can Account B delegate the permissions it received from Account A to users in its own account. Permissions can be granted by an ACL, a bucket policy, or a user policy. Granting permissions to IAM roles is a better practice than granting permissions to individual users.

Account A can also directly grant a user in Account B permissions using a bucket policy. Even then, the user in Account B needs permission from the parent account, Account B. A user can access the resource only when both conditions hold: the user has permission from the resource owner and the user has permission from the parent account.

## How the walkthrough works

The walkthrough does not use root user credentials. Instead, it uses an administrator user in each account to create resources and grant permissions. The tasks of creating users and granting permissions are done in the AWS Management Console. The AWS CLI and AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell are used to verify permissions.

The Account A administrator attaches a bucket policy granting cross-account permissions to Account B. That policy grants s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket permissions to Account B. Because the bucket policy grants these permissions to Account B, the administrator user in Account B automatically inherits them.

The Account B administrator creates user Dave in Account B. The Account B administrator then attaches a user policy to Dave, delegating the permissions received from Account A. This must happen before Dave can list the bucket. Dave's inline policy allows only s3:ListBucket on the bucket.

## Verifying Dave's access

Dave can list the contents of the bucket owned by Account A only when both the bucket policy grants Account B the permissions (s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket) and Dave's inline policy allows s3:ListBucket. Dave has no permissions other than s3:ListBucket, so when Dave runs get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, Amazon S3 returns permission denied.

## Optional test: explicit deny

An explicit deny in a bucket policy or user policy takes precedence over any other permissions. To test this, the bucket policy explicitly denies Account B the s3:ListBucket permission. As a result, Account B and its users cannot list objects in the bucket, and access is denied for AccountBadmin listing the bucket in the explicit deny test.

After the test, the bucket policy again grants Account B the s3:ListBucket permission; Account A's bucket policy allows Account B s3:ListBucket access.

# Cross-account bucket permissions walkthrough

## Before you begin

You need the following in place before starting:

- Two AWS accounts, Account A and Account B (steps on this page).
- An administrator IAM user, AccountAadmin, in Account A with a full-access user policy. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_users_create.html
- An administrator IAM user, AccountBadmin, in Account B with a full-access user policy. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_users_create.html
- The AWS CLI or AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell installed, with profiles/credentials set up for AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/policy-eval-walkthrough-download-awscli.html

## Background

An AWS account can grant another AWS account permission to access its resources, such as buckets and objects. Once Account B has received permissions from Account A, Account B can delegate them to users in its own account, so the first grant must happen before the delegation. Account A can also directly grant a user in Account B permissions using a bucket policy. In that case the user in Account B still needs permission from the parent account, Account B.

Permissions can be granted by an ACL, a bucket policy, or a user policy. Granting permissions to IAM roles is a better practice than granting permissions to individual users.

For a user to access the resource, the user must have permission from the resource owner and permission from the parent account. The user can access the resource only when both hold.

## How the walkthrough works

The Account A administrator attaches a bucket policy granting cross-account permissions to Account B. The administrator user in Account B automatically inherits the permissions granted to Account B; the bucket policy's grant of s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket to Account B is enough for this. Only after that bucket policy is attached does the Account B administrator attach a user policy to the user, delegating the permissions received from Account A.

The walkthrough does not use root user credentials. It uses an administrator user in each account to create resources and grant permissions, which is sufficient to avoid root credentials. The tasks of creating users and granting permissions are done in the AWS Management Console. The AWS CLI and AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell are used to verify permissions.

## Create user Dave and verify access

The Account B administrator creates user Dave in Account B. Dave has an inline policy allowing only s3:ListBucket on the bucket. That policy must be attached, delegating the permissions from Account A, before Dave can list the bucket.

Dave can then list the contents of the bucket owned by Account A. This works only when the bucket policy grants the needed permissions to Account B (s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket) and Dave's inline policy allows s3:ListBucket.

Dave does not have any permissions other than s3:ListBucket. When Dave runs get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, Amazon S3 returns permission denied.

## Optional test: explicit deny

An explicit deny in a bucket policy or user policy takes precedence over any other permissions. In this test, the bucket policy explicitly denies Account B the s3:ListBucket permission. As a result, Account B and its users cannot list objects in the bucket, and access is denied for AccountBadmin listing the bucket. The explicit deny is enough to cause this denial.

To restore access, the bucket policy again grants Account B the s3:ListBucket permission, so that Account A's bucket policy allows Account B s3:ListBucket access.
